pass_a_gloss: Tome 4. [Lemma, Isaiah 36:1-2:] And it happened in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah reigning, Sennacherib king of Assyrians went up against the strong cities of Judaea, and took them. And the king of Assyrians sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem to the king Hezekiah, with a great force, and he stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, in the road of the field of the fuller. The account is clear to all those more fond of learning history; but nevertheless I will tell, speaking briefly as is possible. Ahaz reigning in Jerusalem, then Pekah son of Remaliah and Rezin the king of Syria besieging Judaea, and having planned to lay the hand also on Jerusalem itself, the one mentioned, having become slack toward resistance, was sending an embassy, and indeed was calling to help Tiglath-pileser king of Assyrians, and persuades him with many gifts both to defend him and to cut back the greeds of the kings who had agreed together against him, of that of Samaria I mean and that of Syria. And this having happened, those making war on him perished. For the Assyrian took both Damascus and Syria, and Ahaz came under his hand, and under tribute and taxes from then on. And he was among the very most base. For he was an idolater and God-hated, and perhaps had conquered all the others in the perversities against God. And Ahaz having ended the human life, Hezekiah reigned in place of him, being his son, but a man dear to God, and having fastened on himself the glories of the highest righteousness and piety. This one rebelled, it says, against the king of Assyrians. For he did not endure to let his own kingdom come under tributes, as indeed also Ahaz. For the sake of this cause Sennacherib the king of the Assyrians, as owing to have under tributes both all Judaea and the very kingdom among them, was kindled into angers, and having ravaged Samaria he let loose the army upon the cities throughout Judaea, and having taken many, he sends Rabshakeh at last against Jerusalem itself, not, for the time, to move weapons by law of war, but rather by threats and promises toward gentleness to bait the common people. [Lemma, Isaiah 36:3:] And there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah the steward, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder.
pass_b_english: Tomos 4. “And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of the reign of Hezekiah that Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came up against the fortified cities of Judea and took them. And the king of the Assyrians sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a great army; and he stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller's field” (Isaiah 36:1-2).

The account is plain to all who love to learn history; yet I will tell it, as briefly as I can. While Ahaz was reigning in Jerusalem, Pekah son of Remaliah and Rezin king of Syria were besieging Judea and planning to lay their hands on Jerusalem itself. Ahaz, too weak to resist, sent an embassy and called to his aid Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, and with many gifts persuaded him to help him and to check the greed of the kings who had banded together against him, I mean the king of Samaria and the king of Syria (2 Kings 16:5-9).

When this was done, those who were making war on him perished. For the Assyrian took Damascus and Syria; and Ahaz came under his hand, and from then on under tribute and taxes. He was one of the very worst. He was an idolater and hateful to God, and perhaps surpassed all the others in his perversity toward God.

When Ahaz ended his human life, Hezekiah reigned in his place. He was his son, but a man dear to God, who had won the glories of the highest righteousness and piety. He, it says, “rebelled against the king of the Assyrians” (2 Kings 18:7); for he would not let his kingdom be brought under tribute, as Ahaz of course had done.

For this reason Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, as though he had the right to hold all Judea, and its very kingdom, under tribute, was inflamed with anger. He laid waste Samaria and sent his army against the cities of Judea, and when he had taken many of them, he then sent Rabshakeh against Jerusalem itself, not to take up arms for the time being by the law of war, but rather to lure the common people with threats and with promises of gentle treatment.
“And there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the steward, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder” (Isaiah 36:3).

choices.why: Ahaz, the one just mentioned, lacks strength to resist and sends for Assyrian help.

choices.english: rebelled against the king of the Assyrians
choices.why: 2 Kings 18:7: Hezekiah threw off Assyrian rule.
δελεάζω is to bait a trap; Rabshakeh tries to win the people by threats and promises.
Set against Ahaz, θεομισής, hateful to God.

choices.why: The account is known to the studious; Cyril still tells it briefly.
